# `ontology.grounding.source.columns.<name>`

[ontology](../../../../README.md) · [grounding](../../../README.md) · [source](../../README.md) · [columns](../README.md) · <name>

EVERYTHING ABOUT ONE COLUMN, ON THE COLUMN. Five keys: `offers` (required — what a question may do with it), `references` (the concept its values identify), `value_register` (where its values come from), `rulings` (what a person decided about its relation to another column). `additionalProperties: false` is the point: a misspelled flag is a LOAD ERROR, where a misspelled sentence is just another sentence.

- [`offers`](#offers) — *object* **·** required
- [`references`](#references) — *string*
- [`rulings`](#rulings) — *object*

### `offers`

*object* · **required** · [has its own keys →](offers/README.md)

WHAT A QUESTION MAY DO WITH THIS COLUMN — a map from each use to that use's own terms. An EMPTY map is a statement: the column is loaded, typed, and offered to no question. An ABSENT `offers` is a column nobody classified, which is a finding rather than a state. It was `roles:` until 2026-10-07; the word changed because `role` is what the five DERIVED names are still called and this container is not those names.

Its own keys: [`ontology.grounding.source.columns.<name>.offers`](offers/README.md)

### `references`

*string* · optional

THIS COLUMN'S VALUES IDENTIFY ONE ROW OF THAT CONCEPT — a foreign key, named by the concept it points at. It was `roles: {identity: reference}`, which said only THAT the column pointed somewhere: the target was recovered by matching column names against concepts whose key is that column, and that inference has been observed to fail. `columns[].references` is also the data plane's own measured spelling of this fact (operator ruling, 2026-09-27), so both planes now name it the same way. Whether every value is present over there is a measurement, never a declaration.

### `rulings`

*object* · optional · [has its own keys →](rulings.md)

WHAT A PERSON DECIDED ABOUT THIS COLUMN'S RELATION TO ANOTHER COLUMN. Every member names one: `label_of`, `finer_than` and `scoped_by` take a column name, and `sort` orders this column's own values. `never_axis` left this block on 2026-10-07 because it named no other column — it is `offers.suppressed`.

**When you would reach for it.**

SOMETHING TRUE ABOUT THE COLUMN CANNOT BE MEASURED FROM IT. That is the whole test, and it is the one that tells a ruling from a fact: if profiling the rows could establish it, it is not a ruling and does not belong here. The compelling case is two columns that are 1:1 where one is the other's NAME — cardinality is the same in both directions, so nothing in the data says which is the name and which is the thing.

Its own keys: [`ontology.grounding.source.columns.<name>.rulings`](rulings.md)

### `value_register`

*string* · optional

THE FILE WHOSE ROWS ARE THIS COLUMN'S VALUES, bundle-relative — so a question naming a member by word resolves to the exact value the column holds instead of probing. It was `register`, one word that also named `rulings.register`, a closed five-term enum, one nesting level away: country.yaml declared both seven lines apart. The runtime had already been forced to split them (`value_register` / `naming_register`); the author was still asked to use one word.
